prompt: You've just cloned a large, unfamiliar codebase. What should you do before reading any implementation file?
choices: Read README.md and CONTRIBUTING.md (and ARCHITECTURE.md if present) to learn intent and local conventions
Open the largest file in the repo, since it's likely the most important
Rewrite one module in your preferred style to see how the tests react
Skip straight to the issue tracker and pick any open bug

prompt: Why are a project's tests useful as documentation of intended behavior?
choices: They're always kept perfectly in sync with a written spec document
They encode, in executable form, the specific behaviors maintainers cared enough to protect — including contracts the implementation doesn't state explicitly
They replace the need to ever read CONTRIBUTING.md
They guarantee the code has no bugs

prompt: A code comment looks odd and you want to know why it was written that way. What's the most direct way to find out?
choices: Delete it and see if any test fails
Ask in the project's chat and wait, without checking history first
Use git blame on that line, then git log -p on the file to read the commit and linked discussion that introduced it
Assume it's dead code and remove it in your first PR

prompt: Which issue is best described as a 'trap' rather than a well-scoped good-first-issue?
choices: One file named, a specific function, a concrete expected output, and a maintainer comment describing exactly what to add
Opened 14 months ago, vague ('the CLI should be more intuitive'), no maintainer reply, and multiple commenters proposing conflicting redesigns
Has a clear reproduction case and is labeled 'good first issue' with a recent maintainer triage comment
Scoped to a single small function with an existing test file to extend

prompt: Before writing any code for a good-first-issue candidate, what should you do?
choices: Nothing — just open a PR once it's done, since that's the fastest way to show initiative
Comment on the issue to confirm it's still wanted, briefly state your approach, and ask to be assigned
Fork the repo, implement it, and open a PR without commenting on the issue at all
Wait for the maintainer to assign it to you without any comment from you

prompt: In a GitHub pull request description, what does writing 'Fixes #482' actually do?
choices: Nothing functional — it's purely a stylistic convention with no effect
It automatically closes issue #482 when the PR is merged
It prevents the PR from being merged until issue #482 is manually closed
It assigns issue #482 to the PR author

prompt: A maintainer requests a change on round two of review, and you disagree with it. What's the most constructive response?
choices: Silently ignore the comment and hope it isn't blocking
Make the change without comment to avoid conflict, even though you think it's wrong
Explain your reasoning with concrete evidence (a test case, a benchmark, a relevant doc line) rather than just repeating your original code
Close the PR since disagreement means it won't be merged

prompt: During an active review with multiple rounds of feedback, what's the recommended git workflow?
choices: Force-push a rewritten history after every single review comment
Push new commits addressing each round of feedback, and only squash/rewrite history later if the maintainer asks or the project's process calls for it
Open a brand new PR for each round of feedback
Wait until all feedback across all rounds is collected, then submit one massive final commit with no incremental pushes
